fact_check.fact: Semorinemab reduced cognitive decline by 42.2% on the ADAS-Cog11 at week 49.
fact_check.note: Matches paper Table 2 (treatment difference −2.89 points, p = 0.0008).

fact_check.fact: Semorinemab engaged peripheral tau targets but did not slow brain tau accumulation.
fact_check.note: Paper Results confirm >20-fold increase in plasma tau (Figure 3) but Table 2 confirms no treatment difference in annualized whole cortical gray PET SUVR change (p = 0.9941).

fact_check.fact: The Lauriet trial cohort was strictly 'moderate' severity, meaning the paper's 'mild-to-moderate' label is a discrepancy.
fact_check.note: The clinical-trials researcher incorrectly flagged this. Paper Table 1 shows 90% of the cohort had a CDR-Global Score of 1 (mild AD) and only 10% had a 2 (moderate). The population is accurately described as mild-to-moderate.

research_page.title: Semorinemab in mild-to-moderate AD (Lauriet)
research_page.description: Phase 2 trial showing an isolated cognitive benefit for semorinemab that is widely considered a statistical artifact due to a lack of functional or biomarker efficacy.
research_page.takeaway_md: In the Phase 2 Lauriet trial, the anti-tau antibody semorinemab significantly slowed cognitive decline on the ADAS-Cog11. However, the trial failed its functional coprimary endpoint and all secondary clinical and biomarker measures, leading experts to view the isolated cognitive signal as a false positive.
key_findings_md: Reduced cognitive decline by 42.2% on the ADAS-Cog11 at week 49 compared to placebo (p = 0.0008) (paper, Table 2).
Failed to show a significant treatment effect on the functional ADCS-ADL scale or on global clinical measures like CDR-SB and MMSE (paper, Table 2).
Did not alter the rate of tau accumulation on PET imaging or cerebral atrophy on MRI (paper, Table 2).
Elevated plasma tau biomarkers >20-fold, demonstrating peripheral target engagement without downstream disease modification (paper, Results).
research_page.methods_md: Multicenter, randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled Phase 2 trial of 272 adults aged 50–85 with probable mild-to-moderate AD. Participants received 4,500 mg IV semorinemab or placebo every four weeks for 48 or 60 weeks. Registered as [NCT03828747](https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT03828747).
research_page.trial_evidence_md: This paper reports results from the Phase 2 [Lauriet](/trials/semorinemab-lauriet-nct03828747) trial. The broader clinical evidence for semorinemab as a disease-modifying therapy is very weak. Despite Lauriet's isolated cognitive hit, a larger Phase 2 trial in earlier-stage AD ([Tauriel](/research/papers/semorinemab-tauriel)) unambiguously failed its primary endpoint, leading to the program's apparent discontinuation.
research_page.sentiment_md: Public perception briefly diverged from the scientific evidence when early corporate press releases highlighted the isolated cognitive signal, sparking a retail stock rally for AC Immune. However, the scientific and medical communities remained highly skeptical, recognizing that cognitive benefits without functional or biomarker improvements likely represented a statistical artifact.
caveats_md: The study cohort was predominantly White (89%) and lacked racial and ethnic diversity, limiting the generalizability of the findings.
The COVID-19 pandemic caused missed doses and altered assessment protocols, which could introduce unaccounted variance despite preplanned sensitivity analyses.
A post-hoc analysis revealed the cognitive benefit was driven primarily by a single 'word recognition' item, undermining confidence in the drug's true clinical efficacy.
relates_to_md: [Tauriel Phase 2 trial](/research/papers/semorinemab-tauriel) — Semorinemab's parallel Phase 2 trial in prodromal-to-mild AD, which failed to show clinical efficacy.
[Amyloid hypothesis](/research/amyloid-hypothesis) — Context for targeting tau versus amyloid in disease-modifying Alzheimer's therapies.

trial_pages.title: Lauriet (Semorinemab Phase 2)
trial_pages.description: Phase 2 trial of the anti-tau monoclonal antibody semorinemab in mild-to-moderate Alzheimer's disease.
trial_pages.primary_endpoint: Change from baseline in cognitive function (ADAS-Cog11) and functional capacities (ADCS-ADL) at week 49
trial_pages.why_md: Lauriet tested whether targeting the N-terminal domain of tau could slow disease progression in patients who already exhibit mild-to-moderate symptoms, attempting to establish efficacy in later disease stages after early-stage failures.
status_log_md: **2023-10-03** — Full trial results published in Neurology, showing conflicting cognitive and functional outcomes.
trial_pages.results_md: The trial reported a 42.2% reduction in cognitive decline on the ADAS-Cog11, but failed to demonstrate any benefit on the ADCS-ADL functional scale, secondary clinical measures, or tau accumulation. The isolated cognitive result is widely viewed as a statistical artifact.

notes_for_editor: The clinical trials researcher incorrectly claimed the Lauriet cohort was strictly 'moderate' based on the MMSE 16-21 score, but the paper explicitly states 90% of the cohort had a CDR-Global Score of 1, meaning they actually had mild AD. I corrected this discrepancy and removed their flag.
